newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - No science in Australia gold sales - RBA.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - No science in Australia gold sales - RBA.

text.p: Australia's central bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), said there was nothing "scientific" about its decision to unload 167 tonnes of gold -- 67.6 percent of its total reserves -- onto the market in the last six months to buy foreign currency.

"We looked at it and we decided we needed to hold some gold and the current holdings is about what we decided on, nothing more scientific than that," Ric Battellino, Assistant RBA Governor for financial markets, told Reuters.

"Obviously, in the early 1990s, when the Aussie (Australian dollar) was under downward pressure and it could have been destabilised, we couldn't be seen selling the gold then because people might have seen it as an act of desperation," Battellino said.

"Similarly, when the government budget was not in very good shape it also had the chance or risk of being perceived incorrectly, seen as a chance for the government to get its hands on some Reserve Bank money," Battellino said.
He said the actual sales were made in 1996, when the international gold price was higher than it is now.

Battellino said the sales, which reduce Australia's official gold hoard to 80 tonnes, or 2.57 million ounces, from 247 tonnes, or 7.94 million ounces, were being contemplated by the RBA "for some time."
Proceeds from the sales were used to immediately buy government securities denominated in U.S. dollars, German marks and Japanese yen.

In announcing the gold sales, the RBA said it could no longer justify holding so much gold, given Australia's vast in the ground gold reserves. Australia mines nearly 300 tonnes of gold a year, making it the world's third largest producer.
Gold is currently trading at around four-year lows, battered by investment fund selling and a growing perception that the world's central banks are less interested in holding gold in their reserves.
In the last five years, a number of central banks have sold gold, the most prominent being those of Austria, Belgium, Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal and South Africa.
Battellino said the RBA started selling gold in the middle of the last financial year (July/June) "certainly well into 1996."
At least for now, there are no further sales planned by the RBA, he said. "For the moment we're quite happy to have a bit of gold around."
The gold was sold through "regular channels" in an orderly way so as not to disrupt the market, Battellino said.
"It was just dispersed into the market," he said.

As a result of the sales, while Australia's value of gold holdings fell by A$1.830 billion in June, the value of foreign exchange rose by A$2.368 billion, also taking into account other factors such as valuation changes, the bank said.
